title: Ep 301: From Law Student Startup Founder to Global CEO: Daniel Lewis's Legal Tech Journey
author: Daniel Lewis

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes

kp.k: Earlier startups pressured incumbents without displacing them
kp.d: Lewis attributes the 2012–2014 legal research startup wave to recovering venture investment, interest in vertical software, established incumbents and emerging technology. He says Ravel and other challengers did not disrupt Lexis and Westlaw, but demonstrated capabilities that pressured incumbents to innovate. His estimate that Casetext had 10 to 15 million dollars in revenue at acquisition is presented as his recollection, not documented financial evidence.
qs: there was a wave of funding right in that moment of like 2012 through 2014 where several new challengers got off the ground
none of which ended up disrupting Lexis and Westlaw.

But I think by demonstrating new capabilities, new features, they did put pressure on the large companies to innovate in different ways and sort of showed possibilities to customers of ways in which new value could be created.

kp.k: Authoritative legal data remained a barrier to entry
kp.d: Lewis says Ravel initially expected court digitization to supply sufficient case law, but exhausted available internet material within about six months. Its partnership with Harvard funded digitization of a collection of 40,000 plus reporter books in exchange for temporary commercial exclusivity and eventual public availability. This account identifies comprehensive, authoritative content as an obstacle distinct from software development.
qs: within about six months, we had hoovered up everything that we thought existed on the internet.
they had a full complete collection of 40,000 plus law reporter books
if you guys can fund this, we'll digitize it.
So Harvard can one day make it fully publicly available to everybody. And for a period of time, Ravel Law would have kind of commercial exclusivity to it.

kp.k: Public case law supports models but needs updating
kp.d: Lewis reports that Harvard received interest from foundation-model developers when the Case Law Access Project became fully accessible. He assumes rather than establishes that the data entered major models. He identifies trustworthy, comprehensive ongoing updates as an unresolved problem and says the collection is current only until a few years before the interview.
qs: So I think it's safe to assume all that data has been sucked into the large foundational models now.
how do you keep these things updated on a go-forward basis in a trustworthy and comprehensive way?
the content is at least up to date until a few years ago.

kp.k: Contract review targets in-house efficiency rather than outsourced delivery
kp.d: Lewis positions LegalOn as software for in-house teams, explicitly contrasting it with technology-enabled services that return human-reviewed contracts. He says mature contract lifecycle management had not solved the task-level problem of speeding review. As of the late-August 2025 interview, he reports over 7,000 business users worldwide and customer-reported time savings of up to 85 %, without providing a sample, measurement method or independent validation.
qs: Contract lifecycle management had by that point been around for more than a half dozen years.
it was not solving this problem of how do lawyers actually speed up the task of contract review.
LegalOn is pure software.
So today we're serving over 7,000 businesses around the world and people are reporting up to 85 % time savings on contract review.

kp.k: Attorney playbooks underpin LegalOn's claimed differentiation
kp.d: Lewis says LegalOn combines AI with researched, maintained playbooks containing review issues, corrective language and explanatory practice notes. Lawyers can initiate AI redlines grounded in that content. He argues this reduces implementation effort and makes results more trustworthy than general-purpose ChatGPT; this is a vendor assertion rather than demonstrated elimination of errors.
qs: off the shelf playbooks that are deeply um researched, kept updated, and thorough to cover the issues that in-house teams care about when reviewing a wide array of contracts.
We've drafted language that you can use to correct that issue. And we've drafted a practice note that explains why this matters.
just click a button and we'll use AI to make the red line for you grounded in all of that trustworthy content.

kp.k: Playbook adoption varies with legal department maturity
kp.d: Lewis distinguishes smaller teams lacking resources to develop broad playbook coverage from larger departments with established Word or spreadsheet guidance. LegalOn offers off-the-shelf playbooks, conversion of existing guidance into AI issue spotting and redlining, and combinations of customer and vendor content. He presents this flexibility as a response to differing organizational resources and maturity.
qs: a company with two lawyers might have never made the investment in having playbooks
How do you turn this playbook that's written for humans into something that AI can understand the context of and perform spotting issues and making red lines in the way that you want?
I want to use Legalon's playbook for 80 % of it. And then I'm going to layer on my own playbook and cover the last 20%.

kp.k: Document handling determines whether automation actually saves work
kp.d: Lewis argues that much of the value lies beyond simple NDAs, in complex service, procurement, building and energy contracts. Tables, appendices and unusual formatting can undermine AI processing and redlining. He says successful handling allows users to move quickly, while failures generate manual correction and checking work.
qs: most of the value in this space is unlocked when you're looking at things that are not NDAs.
those contracts, turns out have tables and funky formats and appendices
if you don't get them right, Then folks end up just spinning their wheels and having to kind of manually correct and double check everything.

kp.d: Lewis attributes LegalOn's AI redlining capability to LLM advances and describes further deployed functions: contract question answering, redline summaries, key-term extraction, missing-placeholder detection and translation. He also reports improved issue-spotting accuracy, without supplying task-specific results.
qs: one of the first things that we launched was AI redlining.
And that was unlocked by LLMs having this capability.
You can summarize red lines that have been made. You can extract key terms. You can spot missing placeholders. You can run translations across countless different languages.

kp.k: Human legal expertise remains central to product development
kp.d: Lewis argues that lawyers evaluating and training AI, together with legal content and engineering, improve performance over foundation models alone. He reports double digit percentage improvements on LegalOn's own contract-review benchmark, but supplies no sample size, scoring method or detailed results. Experienced in-house practitioners draft and maintain playbooks as laws and market standards change; this is product maintenance and evaluation, not a claim that every user output receives human verification.
qs: lawyers who are evaluating and training AI to do things in a particular way yields very significant improvements over like what you can get from these LLMs just off the shelf.
double digit percentage improvements
we have a team of attorneys, all experienced in-house practitioners with specializations in different areas
maintaining them as laws and market standards change, but having humans doing that work and applying their judgment.

kp.k: Legal AI competition increasingly crosses established product categories
kp.d: Lewis says the ChatGPT era increased investment, vendor entry and customer interest while dissolving traditional category boundaries. He views the resulting market energy positively overall, but emphasizes the difficulty customers face comparing a noisy array of tools. For founders, he describes greater capital availability and demand alongside greater difficulty attracting attention.
qs: there are a lot more companies, there's a lot more investment flowing into the space.
the sort of dissolving of traditional category lines.
I've never seen customers in the market so interested in. in like leaning into technology as of the last three years.
It's harder to break through. It's harder to gain attention for new ideas in some ways.

kp.k: Funding supports application-layer development and global expansion
kp.d: Discussing the approximately late-July 2025 announcement, Lewis reports a Goldman Sachs-led $50 million Series E, around $200 million raised overall and about 600 employees globally. He says the funding supports global growth and AI development. The OpenAI collaboration deepens an existing relationship through earlier model access and engineering cooperation; LegalOn's strategy is legal-specific development atop foundation models rather than building its own.
qs: the $50 million raise was led by Goldman Sachs. It was our series E round. So now we've raised around $200 million in total. Our team is about 600 people globally.
we're getting sort of earlier access to models as those come out and more side-by-side development on leading edge features with their engineering team.
we don't think the right investment is to build a foundational model ourselves.

This is a prospective product-performance claim, not a reported controlled test.

kp.k: Intake agents automate information gathering before legal work
kp.d: Lewis describes an already launched intake agent that parses emailed requests, identifies missing information, follows up with requesters and prepares matters for legal handling. He distinguishes this from downstream possibilities such as automatically answering some requests using company knowledge or routing them into contract review. His framing is task automation that frees lawyers for decisions, leadership and judgment, rather than a forecast of lawyer headcount reductions.

our intake agent will automatically go back to that requester, parse through the email saying, okay, here's what you did give us. Here's what you didn't. Please answer these other questions.
you can imagine lots of possibilities downstream of that.
automate them away so that lawyers can go back to kind of making decisions, providing leadership, exercising judgment.

kp.k: Expansion centers on broader in-house workflow time savings
kp.d: Lewis says LegalOn has expanded into matter management and plans offerings for managing contracts after signature, with some roadmap developments anticipated over the next three to four months. He characterizes these as responses to longstanding customer problems newly addressable with AI, with time savings as the guiding objective.
qs: We'll have offerings coming out to help manage contracts after they've been signed.
those are a couple of things to look for in the next three to four months or so.
Our North Star is like finding ways to save in-house legal teams time.
this is not technology in search of a problem.

kp.k: Lewis predicts faster professional change over the coming decade
kp.d: Lewis forecasts more change in legal practice over the next 10 years than in the preceding 10, while expressly declining to predict what practice will look like across large and small firms and other client settings. The interview supplies an expectation of accelerated transformation, not specific findings about staffing, leverage, pricing or professional regulation.
qs: I don't have a crystal ball about what legal practice will look like 10 years from now
I'm pretty confident that the change we're going to experience in the next 10 years is a lot more than the change that we experienced in the last 10 years.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Daniel Lewis claims AI substantially accelerates in-house contract review and increasingly automates surrounding legal workflows.
pts.d: Lewis reports customer time savings of up to 85% using LegalOn. He says LLMs enabled automated redlining and now support contract questions, redline summaries, key-term extraction, identification of missing placeholders, translation and improved issue spotting. He distinguishes LegalOn as software used directly by legal teams, rather than a service that receives contracts and returns human-reviewed work. His framing is primarily augmentation: software speeds lawyers' work so they can concentrate on decisions, leadership and judgment, rather than replacing lawyers.

pts.k: Lewis claims attorney-developed content and legal-specific engineering improve AI reliability and reduce the effort required to obtain useful contract-review results.
pts.d: Lewis argues that researched playbooks, suggested language and practice notes ground issue spotting and redlining more reliably than unmodified general-purpose LLMs. He claims lawyer evaluation and training, together with engineering, yield double-digit percentage improvements on LegalOn's contract-review benchmark. He also argues that handling tables, appendices, unusual formatting and stylistically appropriate redlines is necessary to realize time savings; otherwise users must manually correct and check results. His claims of trustworthiness are product claims, not an explicit claim that human verification is unnecessary.

pts.k: Lewis predicts agents will compress playbook conversion from weeks to minutes and automate multi-step intake work.
pts.d: The proposed playbook agent parses a customer's human-readable guidance, identifies positions and fallback language, asks clarifying questions and presents an interpretation for user confirmation before ingestion. Lewis describes an already launched intake agent that identifies missing information in emailed requests, follows up with requesters and prepares matters for the legal team. Automatic responses using company knowledge and transitions into contract review are described as downstream possibilities rather than fully established capabilities.

pts.k: Lewis claims the generative-AI wave has expanded legal-tech investment, customer interest and competition while weakening traditional product-category boundaries.
pts.d: Lewis describes more entrants and more investment since the ChatGPT revolution, with companies moving into areas outside their previous categories. He regards this as broadly positive but says it makes buyers' selection work harder and makes new businesses compete more intensely for attention. His broader prediction is that legal practice will change more during the next decade than during the preceding decade, without specifying a particular future staffing model, pricing model or displacement outcome.

pts.k: Lewis suggests digitized case law has become foundational-model input, but maintaining current, trustworthy legal data remains an unresolved challenge.
pts.d: Lewis connects the public availability of the Case Law Access Project corpus with demand from foundation-model developers. He infers that the corpus has been incorporated into major models; he does not present this as verified knowledge of each model's training data. He distinguishes access to the historical corpus from the continuing difficulty of obtaining comprehensive and reliable updates.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence offered is Lewis's company experience, customer reports and internal benchmarking, supplemented by product descriptions and market observations.
pts.d: The 85% time-saving figure is attributed to customer reports, with no sample size, methodology, baseline or distribution supplied. The 7,000-business customer count describes adoption rather than independently demonstrating effectiveness. The claimed double-digit benchmark improvements come from LegalOn's own contract-review tasks; the transcript supplies no scores, task breakdown, model versions or independent validation. Lewis says OpenAI models consistently lead for LegalOn's use cases in these tests. Playbook maintenance is supported by his account of specialist in-house practitioners drafting and updating content. Agent speed claims are illustrated through intended workflows, not a reported controlled study. Market-change claims draw on his entrepreneurial and executive experience, and the decade-long forecast is expressly a judgment rather than a detailed projection. His inference about case-law ingestion rests on reported developer interest, not confirmed training disclosures.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview separates current capabilities in August 2025 from near-term product plans and a broad ten-year forecast.
pts.d: Lewis describes contract-review savings and multiple LLM features as current, following his 2022 arrival and subsequent advances. The intake agent is described as launched; the playbook agent appears among agents in development and launching soon. He forecasts additional offerings, including post-signature contract management, within roughly three to four months, while leaving parts of the roadmap unspecified. His next-decade prediction runs approximately to 2035. Claimed productivity and reliability gains depend on appropriate legal content, continuing attorney maintenance as laws and market standards change, and engineering that handles complex documents. Playbook conversion depends on user clarification and confirmation. The 85% figure is an upper-end reported saving, not a universal rate, and the weeks-to-minutes comparison is qualified by playbook size.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries and users are corporate legal departments, with different deployment needs by team size; broader effects extend to business requesters and the legal-tech market.
pts.d: Lewis focuses on in-house teams seeking faster contract review and more efficient matter intake. Small departments may lack resources to develop playbooks, while larger departments may need existing guidance translated into executable AI instructions. Business requesters, such as salespeople, would interact with intake agents to supply missing context. Lawyers are envisaged retaining decision-making and judgment as routine work is automated. Legal-tech buyers face more choice and a noisier selection process; vendors and founders gain funding and demand but encounter greater competition. LegalOn is described as a software vendor, not an ALSP delivering outsourced legal work. The broad decade forecast includes large and small law firms and practice serving individuals, but offers no specific access-to-justice or employment outcome.
